catalog_quote: 3.6.1.1 At least one H-tone in each stem. All noun, verb, adjective, and numeral stems have one H-tone element, whose domain may extend over two or more syllables. Therefore melodies /H/, /HL/, /LH/, and /LHL/ are acceptable, but /L/ is not (as a lexical melody). /HLH/ with two tonal peaks occurs in one loanword (nɔ̀y-sày) héyyɛ̀nɛ́ ‘index finger’. Because there is always an H-tone, tone-dropping controlled by another word or by a suffix is always audible. The constraint does not apply to expressive adverbials, some of which have /L/ melody. [...] [3.6, p.39] I use {…} for stem- or word-level tone overlays, conditioned syntactically or, in the case of verbs, by inflectional category (suffixal or not). [...] However, my suspicion is that YS is moving in the direction of an accentual system similar to those I have found recently in nearby Donno So and Dogul Dom on the plateau, where original /H/ melodies and {H} overlays are replaced by falling /HL/ and {HL}. [...] [3.1.2, p.13] Metrical structure, i.e. relationships between strong and weak positions in a linear syllable sequence, is the basis for Syncope and Apocope (§3.4.3.1-2) and for the raising of a nonhigh short vowel to a high short vowel (which can then disappear by Syncope or Apocope). [...] [3.4.3.1, p.28] This shows that the vowel-deletion rules are more sensitive to word-final position than to a metrically definable position.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Toro So Dogon is not in the catalog. The single title-keyword item, Olsen 1987 'Some aspects of tonal accent in Dogon' (SOAS MA thesis, iv+55 pp., tied by Glottolog to Toro So [dts]), is relevant (accent in this language) but unobtainable: no PDF on dogonlanguages.info or Glottolog, Google Books holds only bibliographic mentions of it (SIL Annual Report 1988, SIL Bibliography 1992, Roncador et al. classification print only (SOAS, London), acquisition priority high because it is presumably the only first-hand accent study of Toro So. Its co-authored summary (Bendor-Samuel, Olsen & White 1989 'Dogon', Niger-Congo Languages pp.169-177) is lending-only on archive.org with search-inside refused. The two open first-hand descriptions already held by the project (Heath 2017 Yorno So grammar; Hantgan 2012 Ibi-so sketch) were re-read: neither contains a word-stress statement; both describe a tone language with at least one H per stem, with Hantgan (p.35) allowing a pitch accent reanalysis (one accent per word) and Heath (p.39) suspecting drift toward an accentual /HL/ system. No stress statement found; records and download logs and appended to there. Note: this compilation's was already exhausted, so searching used automated download/API endpoints only.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Yorno So (Toro So) is described purely as a tone language: each lexical stem carries a tone melody containing exactly one H-tone element (/H/, /HL/, /LH/, /LHL/), overridden by syntactically/inflectionally controlled tone overlays; the grammar has no section on stress or accent and never locates a stressed syllable. The only prominence-related remarks are (i) an unlocated reference to metrically strong/weak positions driving syncope/apocope of short high vowels and (ii) the author's suspicion that the variety is drifting toward an 'accentual' (HL-falling) system like Donno So. Hantgan 2012 (Ibi So) independently notes the one-H-per-word property could be read as pitch accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Expressive adverbials may be all-L (exempt from the one-H constraint); one loanword has /HLH/; /H/-melody words often lower the final syllable toward mid pitch, and /LH/ words are often flattened to level high in isolation (p.39).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone melodies are properties of stems/words; overlays ({L}, {HL}, {H}) are imposed by syntactic controllers and verbal inflection; clause-final intonational effects (pitch drop/prolongation, 'dying-quail') treated separately in 3.7. No word-stress domain is defined.
new_statements.identity_note: Heath 2017 describes Yorno So (yɔ̀rⁿɔ̀:-sɔ̌:, Yendouma village cluster, 14 33.3N 03 14.1W), which Heath treats as a variety of the Toro So group and 'not convinced.. should be assigned to different languages' from Sangha So (p.2-3); Glottolog files it under toro1252. Hantgan 2012 describes Ibi So (Ibi village), another Toro So variety said to be divergent. The classic French material (Calame-Griaule 1965, 1968) describes Sangha So (tɔrɔ sɔ of Sanga). All fall under toro1252 Toro So Dogon.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Yorno So is described as a tone language: every noun, verb, adjective and numeral stem carries exactly one H-tone element, so lexical melodies are /H/, /HL/, /LH/, /LHL/ but never /L/ (except some expressive adverbials). The only 'metrical' section concerns strong/weak syllable positions as the basis for Syncope and Apocope, not stress. Heath adds that YS may be drifting toward an 'accentual system' of the Donno So / Dogul Dom type in which /H/ melodies are replaced by falling /HL/; this is a remark about tone melodies, not about word stress. No statement about stress, its position, or its absence.
new_statements.exceptions: The one-H-per-stem constraint does not apply to expressive adverbials, some of which have /L/ melody; one loanword héyyɛ̀nɛ́ 'index finger' has /HLH/ with two peaks (p.40). Heath notes the /H/ vs /HL/ distinction is hard to hear because all-H words of 2+ syllables lower the final syllable, and /LH/ words are often pronounced with flat high pitch in isolation (p.39).
new_statements.identity_note: Heath's grammar describes the Yorno So variety spoken in the Yendouma village cluster (eastern base of the Bandiagara escarpment); he treats it as a dialect of Toro So (which also covers Sangha So and Ibi So). Olsen 1987 is tagged in Glottolog as Toro So Dogon [dts] generally, not a named village variety.

tone_statements.quote: Like all Dogon languages, it has a phonemic distinction between L and H tone... Importantly, almost all Dogon languages have a ban on lexically /L/ words; this means that the most common overlay, {L}, is always audibly distinct from lexical tone. Additional data are drawn from Ben Tey (Heath 2013a), Jamsay (Heath 2008), Najamba (Heath 2011a), and Yorno So (Heath 2011b). ... In Yorno So (Heath 2011), however, the two diverge... A nonpronominal possessor retains its tone in the face of a c-commanding adjective, as in (54a). Yorno So displays a Ben Tey-like output in this case

tone_statements.quote: There are two phonemic tones, H and L, marked with acute (v́) and grave (v̀) accents, respectively; unmarked syllables are toneless. ... Yorno So differs from Tommo So primarily in the fact that it displays contingent control with the numeral. As first described in §3.2.2, we find that numerals become controllers in the presence of a possessor. In simple combinations with nouns, numerals are non-controllers, as in all Dogon languages that we have worked on ... When a possessor is added, the numeral is able to impose a {L} overlay.

tone_statements.quote: The analysis presented here is broadly valid, mutatis mutandis, for most Dogon languages, including Ben Tey, Nanga, Bankan Tey, Toro Tegu, Jamsay, Tommo So, Najamba, Togo Kan (and related varieties), and Yorno So (and the rest of ‘Toro So’). ... In Ben Tey and the other languages in our sample, open-class stems (noun, adjective, numeral, verb) must have at least one lexical H-tone. Using /…/ to enclose lexical tones, stems may be lexically /H/, /LH/, /HL/, /LHL/, or (rarely) /HLH/, but (using # for ungrammatical) not #/L/.

sources.quote: Each stem must surface with at least one high toned vowel. Since each verb root melody must contain at least one high tone, there is a possibility that the language could be considered pitch-accent instead of tone, with one accent per word.
sources.locator: p.35 (verb-root tone paragraph); section 2.3.7 Tone, pp.9-10
sources.note: No word-stress statement. Describes Ibi-so (a Toro So dialect) as a tone language with unpredictable lexical tone on noun and verb roots, a mostly falling contour on verb stems (root vowel H, final mora L), and phrase-final lowering; notes only that the one-H-per-stem culminativity could support a pitch accent analysis. The word 'stress' does not occur.
